nameStory: The 'arrowwood' name comes from Indigenous peoples who valued viburnums for making arrow shafts because their straight, flexible stems were perfect for the job. The 'downy' part refers to the soft, fuzzy hairs you can feel on the undersides of the leaves and young twigs, distinguishing it from its smooth-leaved cousins.
description: Downy arrowwood is a medium-sized deciduous shrub that typically grows about 6 feet tall, forming dense thickets in the wild. It's part of the large viburnum family, which includes many popular landscape shrubs. In spring, it produces clusters of small white flowers that have a somewhat unpleasant smell, followed by dark blue berries in late summer. The leaves turn beautiful orange-red colors in fall, making it quite showy even though it's not as well-known as other viburnums.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite, simple leaves with prominent veins and coarse teeth along the edges. Run your fingers along the underside - they feel noticeably fuzzy or downy, especially when young. The leaf stems (petioles) are relatively short compared to other arrowwoods.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flat-topped clusters of small white flowers in late spring. While pretty to look at, get close and you'll notice they have a slightly skunky or unpleasant odor - not as sweet as many other flowering shrubs.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Dark blue, almost black berries in small clusters that ripen in late summer. Each berry contains a single flattened stone, and they're quite popular with birds.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a dense, rounded shrub typically 4-8 feet tall with multiple stems from the base. Young twigs often have a downy texture that matches the leaves.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Older stems have gray-brown bark that's relatively smooth. The younger branches retain some of that characteristic downy texture for their first year or two.

habitat: Downy arrowwood prefers woodland edges, thickets, and partially shaded areas with well-drained soil. You'll often find it along forest borders, old field edges, and in areas that get morning sun but afternoon shade. It's quite adaptable to different soil types but seems to do best in slightly acidic conditions typical of New England's forests.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters appear in late spring, usually May, just after the leaves have fully emerged. The flowers have that distinctive slightly unpleasant smell that helps with identification.
seasonality.summer: Fully leafed out with that characteristic downy texture on leaf undersides. Green berries begin forming and gradually ripen to dark blue by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn vibrant orange-red colors, making it quite striking. Dark blue berries are fully ripe and attracting birds. This is when the fall color really makes it stand out.
seasonality.winter: Bare branched with gray-brown bark visible. Look for the multiple-stemmed growth habit and any remaining berry clusters that birds haven't eaten yet.

funFact: Despite being called 'arrowwood,' the Indigenous peoples who used viburnum stems for arrows had to carefully prepare them by straightening them over fire and aging them properly - the fresh wood was actually too flexible and would bend rather than fly straight!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with southern arrowwood and northern arrowwood, but downy arrowwood blooms earlier in spring and has that telltale fuzzy texture on leaf undersides and young twigs. Memory trick: 'Downy' means fuzzy - if the leaves feel smooth underneath, it's probably one of the other arrowwoods.
contextualKnowledge: With 33 recorded observations in New England, downy arrowwood is much less common here than its relatives like southern and northern arrowwood. It's more of a midwestern and southern species that just reaches into our region, so finding one is actually quite special for New England plant enthusiasts.
compareHints: Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems. Northern arrowwood has completely smooth leaves and twigs. The downy texture is really the key feature that sets this species apart from its close viburnum relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.
Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
